chapter_theme: On the mountain Tivittan rouses the lion that has hidden in its cave, tears it apart, and tells Vijayan the harm is gone; then Vijayan, pleased, names for his brother the crystal, lotus pools, elephants and gems that the mountain's beauty offers.

cast.role: the younger prince, called the dark-hued one and the younger
Tivittan's elder brother, called the conch-hued one
the two princes who have come to the mountain
the lion that hides in the cave and is killed
the gods of the sky who watch

712.reading: The fire-maned lion, seeing the heroes who have come, roars like thunder, and the rocks of the mountain split, crumble and turn to powder.
712.event: The lion sees the two princes arrive and its roar shatters the rocks around.

713.reading: The dark-hued prince binds on his anklets, bracelets, crest and curled hair, and the lion is broken by one whose strength is like the lion's own.
713.nuance: The last line is compressed and the word division doubtful: it can be read as the prince's cry and the lion's fall, or as the lion splitting something, so the sense is not fixed.
713.event: Tivittan arms himself for the fight with ornaments tied on and hair bound.

714.reading: With the cliffs crumbling and no place left to flee, the green-eyed lion takes its fierce shape and springs on him, and the red-eyed dark tall one prevails by his speed while Death and the quarters of the sky shake.
714.nuance: The Tamil says the lion 'took a form' (உருவுகொண்டு), which hints at more than an animal; these verses do not say what.
714.event: The lion leaps on Tivittan and he overcomes it by his swiftness.

715.reading: In his leap his feet do not touch the ground, the bracelet-hung arms swing, and his hair, garland and chains rise off his shoulders and neck.
715.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are compressed and the nouns hard to join to their verbs; the sense is the speed of the leap and is held loosely.
715.event: Tivittan leaps so that his feet leave the ground and his ornaments fly up.

716.reading: Trees are torn up by the roots, deer and birds that had run along fall to the ground in terror, and the crests of the mountain break at the touch of his fingertips.
716.event: The force of the hero's blows uproots trees, scatters beasts and breaks the peaks.

717.reading: Clouds close in, rocks of the crest pile together, the forest deity dances for joy, and the one in the lion's form flees into a cave of the bright mountain and hides.
717.nuance: The forest deity's dance is read as joy at the lion's flight; the verb is clipped.
717.event: The lion flees into a cave and hides.

718.reading: The younger prince, great in praised fame, moves fast, the earth shakes and the great mountain trembles, and the lion king who lives in the pit stirs from his sleep.
718.nuance: Verse 717 had the lion fleeing into a cave; here a lion king sleeps in a pit. The text does not say whether one lion or two is meant.
718.event: Tivittan's speed shakes the mountain and wakes the lion in the pit.

719.reading: Angered that the lion hid in the dark cave, the strong one bids it live long and split the great mountain, and stands at the cave-mouth roaring until the world shakes and the hill's echo answers with open mouth.
719.nuance: The first two lines are the taunt, its sarcasm heard in 'live long' (வாழிய); the word division at line 3 joins the speaker's name to the verb.
719.event: Tivittan taunts the hidden lion and roars at the mouth of its cave.

720.reading: At the roar the lion, enraged, blazes at fang and eye, answers in a counter-roar, and the cave and the great mountain split and burst.
720.event: The lion answers the challenge with a roar that bursts the cave.

721.reading: With burning eyes, gaping mouth, bright claws, thick feet, curled mane and gleaming curved fangs, the lion rises out of the darkness of the cave.
721.event: The lion comes out of the cave.

722.reading: Its fearless nature swells with its great strength and fame, as if it were a lion that had scooped up the world, and the gods of the sky tremble.
722.event: The lion comes forth in full might and the gods tremble.

723.reading: As the furious lion rises to drink the blood running from his chest, he treads on its mane, seizes it by the curved fangs in his big hand, and the lion lies torn to strips.
723.event: Tivittan treads on the rising lion, grips its fangs and tears it apart.

724.reading: The gods, with fingers on their lips, marvel that this one has destroyed in anger a lion able to kill a thousand lions, or thousands upon thousands of beasts.
724.nuance: Line 3 is a cry of wonder (ஏ) that the gods use, not a statement by the narrator.
724.event: The gods stand amazed at the killing of the lion.

725.reading: The slain lion's blood runs down the rock with rut-water, broken white tusks and bright pearls, like the Ganga washing down vermilion mud.
725.nuance: The pearls and tusks are the lion's spoil: it had killed elephants.

726.reading: The famed one, neither glad nor amazed, goes to his brother and says that he has put away this harm and they should now go to Podanapuram.
726.nuance: His lack of exultation is the point of line 1; the word is 'harm' (ஏதம்), so the lion is treated as a fault in the land to be removed, not as a rival.
726.event: Tivittan tells Vijayan the harm is removed and proposes returning to Podanapuram.

727.reading: Glad at his younger brother's strength, Vijayan answers that before the flow of this blood is left, they must first see the mountain's low slopes.
727.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are clipped and the exact reason for staying is not clear.
727.event: Vijayan, pleased at Tivittan's strength, asks to see the mountain before leaving.

728.reading: Seeing the mountain's beauty, the younger prince, whose anklets kings praise, marvels with wide eyes, and the conch-hued one begins to answer, kindly, that these are works of great merit.
728.nuance: Line 3 may be Vijayan's own words; the break between narration and speech is not marked.
728.event: Tivittan marvels at the mountain and Vijayan begins to explain what he sees.

729.reading: Vijayan tells the hero that what shows white in the grove, where the wind brings flower-dust and honey-drops and the bees do not stop humming, is no pool but a chamber of crystal.
729.nuance: The word division of the first line and the verb 'kollena' are hard to fix, so the sense is a loose one.
729.event: Vijayan names the crystal walls that look like water.

730.reading: Vijayan says that the pools where bees dark as a bull hum over lotus on stalks, and where silvery fish leap and tear the flowers, are no pools.
730.nuance: Line 3 is the hardest in the passage: its words for the fish and the broad leaf are guesses.
730.event: Vijayan names a mirage of lotus pools on the mountain.

731.reading: Vijayan says that where the hill-side darkens under long drops and men shiver with a roar, the dark shapes in which lightning flashes are no clouds but elephants.
731.event: Vijayan names the elephants that look like clouds.

732.reading: Vijayan says that the white-haired beasts that graze the bean-fields and drink the stream, and drift like young clouds on the great hill, are the yaks moving about.
732.nuance: The addressee is the sea-hued prince, 'kadalvanna' in line 4, which fits Tivittan.
732.event: Vijayan names the yaks that look like clouds.

733.reading: Vijayan says that the bright gems lying where mountain water leaps in the rock hollows glow like a young crescent moon shining in the night sky.
733.nuance: The word division of lines 1 and 2 is broken.
733.event: Vijayan names the gems that glow like moons.

734.reading: Vijayan says that in the dark of the plantains, bamboo and hard-to-see caves, the gems seem to burn with the gold glow of the prince's own ornaments.
734.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 are broken by word division.
734.event: Vijayan likens the mountain's jewels to the prince's ornaments.

links.note: The opening verse promises the tale of the red-eyed one who tore open the lion with the gaping mouth; verse 723 shows the tearing.
links.teaches: The poet's first promise is kept here as a deed in a scene, and the lion in the invocation is now seen as an actual foe.

links.note: Verse 95 sets a fanged beast on the throne gripping an elephant calf as the king's emblem; in 723 the real lion is seized and torn by the prince.
links.teaches: The royal lion of the throne is an image of power, and this verse puts the prince above the beast the throne imitates.

links.note: In 109 those in the hall say Tivittan will guard the whole world under one umbrella; in 722 the gods tremble before the lion he is about to overcome.
links.teaches: What the hall only affirmed of Tivittan's coming rule is tested here by a foe even the gods fear.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 2026 tells of five lions in a forest whose claws and teeth must be cut before the Lord is reached; verse 723 has a prince seize a lion by the fangs and tear it.
links.teaches: The same beast is mastered here by force of arm and there by a cutting of the claws, so the lion stands both for an outer foe and for an inner one.

gains.a: The verse lacks any sense of the lion as something within, which Tirumular's five lions give.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse lacks the act itself, a seizing of the fangs and a tearing, which the epic supplies as a deed.

links.note: Naladiyar 198 holds up the lion's strength as the measure of a man who would die poor rather than shame himself; in 724 the lion is the foe whose strength the gods marvel to see overcome.
links.teaches: The lion is first the model of honour and then the thing a stronger man destroys, so strength is not a single measure.

gains.a: The verse lacks the use of the lion as a standard of honour, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where the lion's own strength is beaten, which the verse shows.

links.note: Kural 774 has the warrior laugh as he pulls a spear from his body; in 726 the victor of a harder fight shows neither joy nor wonder.
links.teaches: The Kural's soldier takes pleasure in the fight and the epic's prince does not, so the same bravery is shown with two moods.

gains.a: The verse lacks the picture of a fighter who delights in the wound, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a hero who is plain after victory and calls it the removal of a harm.

links.note: Kural 382 names fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive as a king's nature; in 719 the prince taunts a lion in its own cave.
links.teaches: The couplet's first quality is shown here as a deed done before a foe with no help, so fearlessness is seen at its cost.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general name for what the prince is doing, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a test of fearlessness against a danger, which the verse supplies.

source_issues: Verses 713, 715, 719, 727, 728, 729, 730, 733, 734: compressed grammar or broken word division make the sense uncertain.
Verses 717 and 718: a lion flees into a cave in 717, and a lion king sleeps in a pit in 718; the text does not say whether it is one lion.
